children: Emma Tucker
1. FROM MY DESK

For a devoted class of credit-card holders, tracking sign-on bonuses and perks has become a full-time obsession. Armed with calendar reminders and viral hacks, they are constantly hunting for ways to milk points. Now, banks are pushing back.

Card companies are clamping down on so-called gamers who they say cross the line and violate their rules. Chase and (Citi) have introduced lifetime bonus limits, while (American Express) uses dedicated analysts to sniff out "rewards leakage" and abuse. Points junkies say they are playing by the rules, but card agreements give issuers broad discretion to seize rewards and shut down accounts.
Ben Glickman and Oyin Adedoyin examine the escalating friction between premium card issuers and the points fanatics testing their limits.

2. TODAY'S HEADLINES

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, aka AOC, has softened her tactics and reached out to voters and lawmakers across factions and party lines. To reach her biggest goals, she'll need to broaden her base without alienating her supporters on the left.
Former President Barack Obama harshly criticized President Trump and Republicans in an Ohio rally.
A group of U.S. executives quit an Alaskan natural-gas startup, alleging they recently learned it was secretly funded by Russian gas giant Novatek.
Washington has tapped exiled opposition lawmaker Dinorah Figuera to negotiate a democratic transition in Caracas, even as Trump embraces the officials she wants to replace.
Kyiv is bracing for its harshest winter of the war as relentless Russian strikes batter the capital's power grid.
3. FROM THE MARKETS

Analysts expect S&P 500 earnings to jump 30% in third-quarter earnings from a year ago, but that corporate profit boom is heavily reliant on just a handful of AI giants. Just 10 companies account for roughly two-thirds of the growth, and many of those are tied to the artificial-intelligence trade. The risk in that concentration lies in whether massive tech spending ultimately delivers.
4. READ IT HERE FIRST
A Texas man fell for an online romance. It turned him into an unwitting money mule.

Garrick Stafford swapped dinner updates and made plans for the future with his glamorous online girlfriend, Sarah-all while draining his savings, running up credit-card debt and moving tens of thousands of dollars into crypto wallets. A South Carolina investigator shattered the illusion: "Sarah" was a married couple in Nigeria taking turns texting him. Stafford's heartbreak reveals a troubling evolution in romance scams. Thieves aren't just taking victims' savings; they're using them to launder money from other schemes through the U.S. financial system. Joe Barrett chronicles Stafford's unraveling and the growing peril of digital love traps.
The Saudi airline that launched right in the middle of a war.

This year was meant to see the arrival of a key pillar in Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's economic ambitions: a high-end airline to funnel wealthy tourists to futuristic desert cities and rival neighbors like Qatar and the U.A.E. Instead, Riyadh Air started commercial flights this summer in the thick of a resurgent conflict. Months after getting off the ground, the airline has evacuated all aircraft from its home base and halted almost all flying after Houthi missile strikes battered the capital. Benjamin Katz and Stephen Kalin report on how the fighting has upended Saudi Arabia's airline industry.

6. SEE THE STORY
How France became the poster child for debt woes.

France has emerged as the biggest victim of rising global bond yields. With little room to raise taxes and voters rejecting austerity, the country's net debt is projected to top 111% of GDP this year, while 10-year yields recently breached 5% for the first time since 2002. Columnist James Mackintosh charts the numbers behind Paris's mounting fiscal crunch.
7. HAPPENING THIS WEEK
Monday: The Ballon d'Or ceremony takes place in London, honoring soccer's top players. Verizon reports earnings.
Tuesday: Israelis vote in a general election. The Federal Reserve begins its two-day policy meeting. U.S. consumer-confidence and durable-goods data are due.
Wednesday: The Fed announces its interest-rate decision. Apple holds a product-launch event in Los Angeles. Microsoft and Alphabet report quarterly earnings.
Thursday: The first estimate of third-quarter U.S. economic growth and the Fed's preferred inflation gauge are released. Amazon reports earnings.
Friday: The U.N. biodiversity summit concludes in Armenia. Exxon Mobil and Chevron report earnings. U.S. employment-cost data are due.
8. THE NUMBER

That's how much searches on (Yelp) for all-you-can-eat buffets jumped in the course of a year, signaling a surge of interest in unlimited dining as diners face economic uncertainty and rising food prices. While traditional chains like Golden Corral continue catering to the budget-minded, newer hot spots-from Korean barbecue to Uzbek delicacies-are pairing value with variety.
9. AND FINALLY...
Here's one place where a thick Boston accent gets you ahead.

Boston's Logan Airport launched a contest last month, looking for someone with a "voice that feels like home" to greet and guide the roughly 130,000 people who fly in and out of the airport every day. More than 5,000 hopefuls lined up to show off their best "lobstahs" and "hahbahs." Judges narrowed it down to eight people. Check out what separated the true locals from the pack.
